Every graph in CausalStructures.jl is stored as a packed CSR (compressed sparse
row) layout. Each node's parents, children, spouses, and neighbors occupy a
contiguous slice of a single flat array, so querying a node's parents requires
only index arithmetic into that array: `parents()`, `children()`, `spouses()`,
and `neighbors()` are effectively O(1) on the Julia side. Many higher-level
algorithms, including `d_separated()`, `ancestors()`, and adjustment-set search,
are built on these primitive operations, so their performance depends directly
on the efficiency of these basic queries.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(CausalStructures)
setup()
warmup()
```

## Queries stay fast as graphs grow

Single-hop queries such as `children()` are just slice lookups on the Julia
side, so their runtime is essentially unchanged whether the graph has 100 nodes
or 10,000:

```{r}
#| label: children-scaling

for (n in c(100, 1000, 10000)) {
  dag <- generate_graph(n, p = 5 / n, seed = 1L)
  node <- paste0("V", n %/% 2)
  t <- bench::mark(children(dag, node), check = FALSE)
  cat(sprintf("n=%-7d children: %s\n", n, format(t$median)))
}
```

The same design carries through the rest of the query layer. Functions such as
`ancestors()`, `d_separated()`, `topological_sort()`, `minimal_separator()`, and
`markov_blanket()` are all built on the same primitive operations and remain
fast on graphs with hundreds of nodes:

```{r}
#| label: multi-query

dag <- generate_graph(500, p = 0.1, seed = 1L)
x <- "V10"
y <- "V290"

rows <- list(
  d_separated = function() d_separated(dag, x, y),
  ancestors = function() ancestors(dag, x),
  topological_sort = function() topological_sort(dag),
  minimal_separator = function() minimal_separator(dag, x, y),
  markov_blanket = function() markov_blanket(dag, x)
)
for (label in names(rows)) {
  t <- bench::mark(rows[[label]](), check = FALSE)
  cat(sprintf("%-20s%s\n", label, format(t$median)))
}
```

## Searching for adjustment sets

`all_adjustment_sets()` (and `all_backdoor_sets()`, `all_iv_sets()`,
`all_frontdoor_sets()`) search subsets of the candidate universe up to
`max_size`, checking each one against the relevant validity criterion.
Consequently, the runtime grows exponentially with `max_size`:

```{r}
#| label: adjustment-sets

admg <- generate_graph(35, p = 0.25, class = "ADMG", latents = 8, seed = 1L)
x <- "V3"
y <- "V33"

for (ms in c(2, 3, 4)) {
  t <- bench::mark(
    all_adjustment_sets(admg, x, y, minimal = FALSE, max_size = ms),
    iterations = 5,
    check = FALSE
  )
  r <- all_adjustment_sets(admg, x, y, minimal = FALSE, max_size = ms)
  cat(sprintf("max_size=%d  %s  (%d sets)\n", ms, format(t$median), length(r)))
}
```

## Advanced algorithms

### Exact uniform DAG sampling

`generate_graph()` uses an Erdős--Rényi model and therefore does not sample
uniformly from the space of DAGs. `uniform_dag()` instead draws exactly
uniformly from all labelled DAGs on `n` nodes:

```{r}
#| label: uniform-dag

for (n in c(10, 20, 40)) {
  t <- bench::mark(
    uniform_dag(n, seed = 1L),
    iterations = 5,
    check = FALSE
  )
  cat(sprintf("n=%-4d%s\n", n, format(t$median)))
}
```

### Markov equivalence class enumeration

`count_dags()` and `enumerate_dags()` operate on a CPDAG/PDAG/MPDAG by
considering every DAG in its Markov equivalence class. The size of that class
grows combinatorially with the number of undirected edges: a clique on `k` nodes
has `k!` consistent orientations, so the class can grow very large very quickly.
`enumerate_dags()` is more expensive than `count_dags()`, since it must
materialize every DAG rather than simply count them:

```{r}
#| label: count-dags

for (k in c(5, 7, 9)) {
  names_k <- paste0("V", seq_len(k))
  spec <- paste(
    combn(names_k, 2, \(p) paste(p[1], "---", p[2])),
    collapse = ", "
  )
  pdag <- cgraph(spec = spec, class = "PDAG")

  n_dags <- count_dags(pdag)
  t_count <- bench::mark(
    count_dags(pdag),
    iterations = 5,
    check = FALSE
  )
  t_enum <- bench::mark(
    enumerate_dags(pdag),
    iterations = 5,
    check = FALSE
  )
  cat(sprintf(
    "k=%d  DAGs=%d  count_dags=%s  enumerate_dags=%s\n",
    k,
    n_dags,
    format(t_count$median),
    format(t_enum$median)
  ))
}
```

### MAG equivalence class enumeration

`enumerate_mags()` is the PAG/MAG counterpart to `enumerate_dags()`, but the
algorithm behind it is not the same: it brute-forces every tail/arrowhead
assignment for each circle endpoint in the PAG (`2^k` candidates for `k` circle
endpoints), validates each candidate as a MAG, and keeps the ones that map back
to the original PAG. There's no analog of Chickering's recursive pruning here,
so it's considerably more expensive than `count_dags()`/`enumerate_dags()` at a
comparable scale:

```{r}
#| label: enumerate-mags

for (k in c(3, 4, 5)) {
  names_k <- paste0("V", seq_len(k))
  spec <- paste(
    combn(names_k, 2, \(p) paste(p[1], "o-o", p[2])),
    collapse = ", "
  )
  pag <- cgraph(spec = spec, class = "PAG")
  n_mags <- length(enumerate_mags(pag))
  t <- bench::mark(
    enumerate_mags(pag),
    iterations = 5,
    check = FALSE
  )
  cat(sprintf("k=%d  MAGs=%d  %s\n", k, n_mags, format(t$median)))
}
```

`count_dags()`, `enumerate_dags()`, `enumerate_mags()`, and the whole
`all_*_sets()` family parallelize their search across Julia threads once the
problem is large enough to benefit, when `JULIA_NUM_THREADS` is set before
loading the package.
